title: A Curious Case of Black Limb in Tuberculosis
case_text:
A 26-year-old male patient, nonsmoker, got admitted with complaints of cough with expectoration of whitish mucoid sputum with no blood streaks, shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain, fever, and loss of appetite over 2 months. The patient had also developed complaints of swelling in the left lower limb for 5 days that was accompanied by blackish discoloration of digits for 2 days [Figure 1]. A history of TB was given 6 months back for which anti-tubercular therapy, involving a combination of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, was taken for 3 months and further lost to follow-up. There was no history of trauma in this patient. The discolouration of the limb was not due to trauma related contusion. There was no change in discoloration on exposure to cold or the presence of rash, joint pains, or photosensitivity.
The patient, on admission, was febrile with a temperature being recorded at 102 F, with a pulse rate of 116/min, blood pressure 94/70 mmHg, SpO2 90% in room air, and a respiratory rate of 26/min. Chest examination revealed decreased breath sounds on the right side with succussion splash. His left lower limb was cold with absent peripheral pulses and discoloration involving the digits and dorsum of the foot and further rapidly spread to involve the calf and up to the knee. Ankle brachial pressure index was noted <0.8. Chest X-ray [Figure 2] proved the presence of hydropneumothorax which was further confirmed by ultrasonographic evaluation and computed tomography (CT) of the thorax. An intercostal tube drainage was done on the right side. The pus so obtained and sputum was evaluated by smear microscopy, and reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) detected the presence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Meanwhile, an arterial and venous Doppler was done for the changes in his lower limb that revealed the presence of reduced flow in anterior and posterior tibial arteries and dorsalis pedis artery with sparing of large peripheral arteries. A CT aortogram was done, which revealed near complete occlusion of the above arteries resulting in an ischemic limb. We dug further for possible etiologies in relation to arterial occlusion, which yielded a negative ANCA antibodies: PANCA 5.16 (<10), CANCA 8.22 (<10), and APLA-related antibodies: 11 U/ml (<15 U/ml) by enzyme immunoassay. Antinuclear antibodies was found to be negative. The rheumatoid (RA) factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody were found to be negative. Serological markers for hepatitis B and C, human immunodeficiency virus were negative. Hemoglobin levels were found to be 7.6 g/dl (indices suggestive of anemia of chronic disease) with a total leukocyte count of 8000 and platelet count of 200,000, PT INR was obtained to be 10 s with an INR of 0.5 (within normal limits), D-dimer was found to be elevated, peripheral smear revealed microcytic anemia with normal platelet count.
In view of the advancing gangrene, amputation was done, and a biopsy sample taken from the amputated specimen showed signs of arterial thrombosis with other signs of gangrene [Figure 3]. The patient was started on anti-tubercular therapy (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol) in view of the microbiological positivity. However, he developed sepsis following surgery, for which he was started on a combination of piperacillin-tazobactam, vancomycin, and levofloxacin apart from fluid, oxygen, and vasopressor support. However, he succumbed to multiple organ damage.
